source: McCaffrey and Spector (2012) Behind every innovative solution lies an obscure feature (Knowledge Management & E-Learning 4(2))
finding: Gap 4. The only numbers I could open for the generic parts technique (GPT) come from this later paper by the same authors, which reports McCaffrey (2012) in one paragraph. People trained to build a parts tree and replace use-implying words with material and shape words solved far more fixation problems than untrained people. No independent replication was found or opened.
numbers: 14 trained vs 14 untrained subjects, 8 insight problems that all depend on functional fixedness. Solution rate 83% vs 49%, t(26)=4.23, p<.001. The press-release figure '67% more' is a rounded relative gain (83/49 = 1.69). My own estimate from t: d about 1.6. Two pilot subjects using a software version solved 8 of 8. Side study: 15 subjects listed features of 14 objects for 4 minutes each; for 20.7 of 32 feature types (64.7%) they gave zero or one response.
limits: Control group got no training and no placebo task, so attention and effort are not matched. Tiny N, no effect size reported. Authors are the technique's inventors. The original Psychological Science paper was not opened (paywall). No replication found. The software pilots are N=2.
agent_relevance: The control rate for a no-technique baseline is about 49% on these problems. A parts-tree prompt is a cheap test, but no LLM result exists. Test it on MacGyver items with matched tokens before adding it as an operator.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) NoveltyBench: Evaluating Language Models for Humanlike Diversity (COLM 2025)
finding: Gaps 1 and 3. Four ways to get diverse answers from the same model were compared: independent resampling, paraphrased prompts, a 'producer of unique answers' system prompt, and in-context regeneration (keep all earlier answers in the chat and ask for a different one). Showing the model its own earlier answers plus an explicit 'different' request was best. So earlier output in context did not cause copying here; with an explicit request it worked as an avoid list.
numbers: 100 curated prompts, 8 generations each, Claude-3 Opus, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.0 Pro; 8 author-written human answers per prompt as baseline. Paraphrasing and system prompt only marginal. In-context regeneration brought all three models roughly to human-writer diversity, and GPT-4o and Gemini 2.0 Pro exceeded humans on cumulative utility. Independent-sampling baseline: 10 samples at temperature 1.
quote: In-context regeneration is the most successful approach, with all three models roughly matching the diversity of human writers
limits: Read from text and a figure; I did not extract per-model numbers. Context grows with each regeneration, so token cost is higher than independent sampling, and no equal-token comparison was run. Utility is a reward-model score, not a human final-pick rating. The human baseline is the authors, not a crowd.
agent_relevance: Keep an explicit log of earlier answers in context and ask for something different. Implicit exposure (Deng, Sinha) harms; explicit exclusion helps. The instruction is the difference.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Verbalized Sampling, method comparison and human study (re-opened for baselines)
finding: Gap 1. This is the closest thing to an equal-budget comparison. Baselines are Direct (N calls), CoT (N calls), Sequence (list k answers in one call, N/k calls), Multi-turn (history kept, N calls), and VS variants, all producing the same total N candidates. On jokes most of the gain of VS over Direct comes from simply listing several answers in one call.
numbers: Human study (Prolific, 90 annotators, 30 per task), diversity on a 1-4 scale, Direct / Sequence / VS-Standard: Poem 1.90 / 2.07 / 2.39; Story 2.74 / 2.76 / 3.06; Joke 1.83 / 2.93 / 3.01. Authors say they controlled the total computing budget but also that VS costs more latency and tokens per call. Gains are 1.5 to 2 times larger on bigger models. Sequence and VS-Standard lowered quality on small models; VS-CoT and VS-Multi did not on large ones.
limits: Measures diversity of the pool and average quality, not the quality of the single best pick, so it does not answer 'best final pick at equal tokens'. 'N controlled' is a count of candidates, not tokens. Critique-and-edit, title-revise-expand and banned-feature lists were not in the comparison. Only creative-writing tasks.
agent_relevance: List-then-pick in one call (Sequence) is nearly as good as VS for jokes and cheaper. A defixation operator should be tested against 'ask for k in one call', not only against single samples.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Verbalized Sampling, inter-annotator agreement (appendix)
finding: Gap 10. Judge noise differs by task and by what is judged. Three human annotators rated 18 output pairs (three comparisons per method on two topics per task).
numbers: Gwet's AC1 for diversity: joke 0.86, story 0.87, poem 0.54. For quality: joke 0.79, poem 0.64, story 0.49. Agreement was defined as at least two of three annotators giving the same score.
limits: Small subset (18 pairs), Gwet's AC1 not kappa, 4-point scale, pairwise similarity rather than an item key. Creative-writing tasks only.
agent_relevance: Diversity of a short formulaic output (joke setup and punchline) is judged reliably; open-ended quality of stories is not. Prefer probes with an answer key or a coded feature over holistic quality ratings.

source: Sinha, Arun, Goel, Staab, Geiping (2026) The Illusion of Diminishing Returns: Measuring Long Horizon Execution in LLMs (ICLR 2026), self-conditioning
finding: Gap 3 (adjacent evidence: errors, not ideas). When the chat history contains the model's own earlier mistakes, the model makes more mistakes later, beyond what long context alone explains. Larger models are not immune.
numbers: Counterfactual design: injected histories with 0, 25, 50, 75 and 100% error rate in earlier turns, then accuracy at turn 100. Qwen3-14B and 32B, Gemma3-12B and 27B: accuracy at turn 100 falls steadily as the induced error rate rises. Frontier non-thinking models (Kimi-K2, DeepSeek-V3, Qwen3-235B-Instruct) are near perfect on a fully correct history but still fall as the error rate rises. Numbers are in figures; I did not extract exact values.
quote: models become more likely to make mistakes when the context contains their errors from prior turns
limits: Task is a simple retrieve-then-compose key-value lookup with one right answer, not idea generation. The effect is copying errors, not copying ideas or features. Controlled study uses open-weight models.
agent_relevance: A failed attempt left in context raises the odds of another failure. Supports dropping raw failed drafts from context and keeping only a short no-good summary. The experiment did not test summaries.

source: Sinha et al. (2026) Illusion of Diminishing Returns, thinking and context removal (Result 5, Appendix C.2)
finding: Gaps 3 and 8. Qwen3 thinking models showed no self-conditioning: turn-100 accuracy stayed stable whatever share of earlier turns was wrong. For non-thinking models, a sliding window that keeps only the last N turns improved performance, and prompting the model to self-verify did not fully fix it. The authors saw that thinking traces do not refer back to earlier answers.
numbers: Qwen3 4B, 8B, 14B, 32B with thinking on vs off, histories with controlled error rates. Sliding window: accuracy improves significantly as the window shrinks (Figure 10a; values not extracted). Without CoT, even the biggest models fail to execute more than a few steps per turn.
limits: Qwen3 thinking was trained by RL with prior traces not shown, so 'thinking' and 'prior traces removed' are mixed. A sliding window only works for tasks without long-range dependencies. Not a creativity task.
agent_relevance: Extra thinking per step can break the pull of earlier output on a checkable task. For creative restarts, drop earlier drafts from context rather than hoping the model ignores them.

source: Kim, Podlasek, Shidara, Liu, Alaa, Bernardo (2025) Limitations of large language models in clinical problem-solving arising from inflexible reasoning (mARC-QA, Scientific Reports)
finding: Gap 8. Items built to trigger the Einstellung effect (a familiar pattern points to the wrong clinical action) were hard for every model, including reasoning models. The reasoning-trained DeepSeek-R1 was only two points above its non-reasoning sibling DeepSeek-V3, and o1 was below both.
numbers: mARC-QA, 100 items; five physicians averaged 66%. Accuracy: DeepSeek-R1 52%, DeepSeek-V3 50%, Gemini-1.5-pro 50%, o1 48%; most other models under 50%, several near or below chance (under 20%). Difference to humans significant (paired bootstrap p=.0133 for V3 and R1, p=.0204 Gemini, p=.0015 o1). Average over 15 runs per model; all LLM prompts used few-shot chain of thought. Models overconfident. On the 20-item human-miss set R1 beat humans in 45% of cases but was confidently wrong 40% of the time.
limits: R1 vs V3 differ in more than thinking, and the 2-point gap has no test of its own. Chain of thought was on for all models, so there is no no-thinking arm. Physician baseline is five people.
agent_relevance: Extra thinking did not cure domain-knowledge fixation. Use a held-out counterfactual item (a case where the usual rule is wrong) as a probe, since it has a fixed key.

source: Ezzat, Camarda, Cassotti, Agogue, Houde, Weil, Le Masson (2017) How minimal executive feedback influences creative idea generation (PLOS ONE 12(6): e0180458)
finding: Gap 2. A human, code-checked analogue of a banned-feature list, applied per idea. Experimenters classified each idea on the egg-drop task as in the fixation path (damp the shock, slow the fall, protect the egg) or in the expansion path. After each idea, 'congruent' feedback said 'search for another path' (fixation idea) or 'continue in this path' (expansion idea). 'Incongruent' feedback said the reverse. Control got a neutral receipt.
numbers: Experiment 1, N=60 (20 per group), 10 minutes, text chat. Condition x path interaction F(2,57)=10.4, p<.001, eta-squared .27. Fixation-path ideas: congruent 5.15 (SD 2.06), control 6.75 (SD 3.85), incongruent 7.85 (SD 3.56); congruent vs control n.s. (corrected p=.12, d=.52); congruent vs incongruent corrected p=.03, d=.92. Expansion-path ideas: congruent 6.75 (SD 5.12), control 4.7 (SD 3.04), incongruent 2.75 (SD 1.71); congruent vs control corrected p=.05, d=.49; control vs incongruent p=.032, d=.79; congruent vs incongruent p=.0005, d=1.05. The abstract's 100 students include a second experiment of 40 on how feedback is interpreted.
limits: Small groups with large SDs. The benefit over control is borderline (p=.05) and the drop in fixation-path ideas is not significant against control; the gain came from more expansion ideas. A trained human coded each idea. One task. Wrong-direction feedback clearly hurts.
agent_relevance: A per-idea check that labels an output as 'old path' and says 'search elsewhere' helps a little. Confirming old-path ideas hurts a lot. Never let the agent reward or elaborate on an item the check marks as old path.

source: Castricato et al. (2024) Suppressing Pink Elephants with Direct Principle Feedback (arXiv 2402.07896)
finding: Gap 2. Telling a language model not to mention an entity often fails, and for weaker chat models it can make the mention as frequent or more frequent. This is the model-side counterpart of the human 'avoid' instructions that did nothing in Jansson and Smith.
numbers: Table 1 (garbled in my text extract, so indicative only): base mention rate 0.33 for the models listed; with an avoid prompt GPT-4 about 0.13 and Llama-2-13B-Chat about 0.25. The authors state OpenHermes baseline models mention the entity 'as often or more often' when told to avoid it. DPF fine-tuning brought OpenHermes to GPT-4-level avoidance. GPT-4 judge agreed with two authors on 200 examples: 98.5% and 94.5%.
limits: Old models (2023), dialogue, avoiding a named entity, not an idea family. About instruction following under a system prompt, not creativity. Table parse uncertain.
agent_relevance: A plain 'avoid X' line is unreliable. A code check on the output (string or category match, then regenerate) is more dependable than relying on the instruction. Cost: one extra call per failure.

source: Wang, Okada, Takagi (2023) How to effectively overcome fixation: a systematic review (Frontiers in Education), avoid instructions
finding: Gap 9. The review lists the human findings on 'avoid' instructions and gives its own explanations for the split. It does not run a test.
numbers: No instruction effect: Jansson and Smith (1991); Viswanathan and Linsey (2013a,b) warnings, with and without explanation; Viswanathan et al. (2014). Effect found: Chrysikou and Weisberg (2005), a replication of Jansson and Smith. Authors' two guesses: (1) group testing in the first study vs individual testing in the replication; (2) psychology students vs engineering students and professional designers. Purcell and Gero (1996): a mechanical-engineering example fixated only mechanical-engineering students.
limits: Secondary source. I did not open Jansson and Smith (1991), Viswanathan, or Chrysikou and Weisberg. Neither explanation has been tested in one design. The review gives no effect sizes.
agent_relevance: Whether an 'avoid' line works may depend on whether the fixation source is the example or deep domain knowledge. For an LLM the analogue is training-set pull, where instructions are expected to be weak.

source: Wang, Okada, Takagi (2023) review, abstraction and format of examples (Atilola 2016, Ezzat 2020, Agogue 2014, Cardoso and Badke-Schaub 2009)
finding: Gap 5. Secondary report of the abstraction results. Primary effect sizes were not available to me.
numbers: Atilola et al. (2016): examples shown as a function tree (text, no specific features) reduced the number of copied features; idea count unchanged; quality higher; the effect vanished when a sketch was added to the function tree. Ezzat et al. (2020): warnings that mention the examples at a higher level of abstraction reduced fixation and raised originality. Agogue et al. (2014): 'expansive' examples reduced fixation and raised originality. Cardoso and Badke-Schaub (2009a): text examples fixated less than pictures; their replication (2009b) found no difference. No numbers are given in the review.
limits: Review text only. I could not open Atilola 2016, Ezzat 2020 or Agogue 2014, and the search APIs were rate-limited. Sketch plus function tree cancelled the benefit, so mixed formats are risky. The picture vs text effect failed to replicate once.
agent_relevance: Giving the agent prior solutions as a function-level description, not the text or code of the answer, is supported by human evidence of unknown size. No LLM test exists.

source: George and Wiley (2020) Need something different? (Memory and Cognition 48:226), Experiment 2 with visual examples
finding: Gap 9. With pictures of common uses, example exposure alone reduced originality (fixation). An avoid instruction removed the drop but did not push originality above the no-example group.
numbers: Experiment 2, 36 per cell, 144 total. Proportion of original ideas: Examples+NoAvoid .38 vs NoExamples+NoAvoid .55, t(70)=2.16, p=.034, d=.51. Examples+Avoid .59 vs the other three cells .47, t(142)=1.81, p=.072, d=.35 (marginal). Count of original ideas, planned Examples+Avoid vs rest: t(142)=1.55, p=.149, d=.29. Experiment 1 (verbal examples) numbers are in a25 and b07: gain only in the Examples+Avoid cell, d=.58.
limits: Psychology undergraduates, individual testing, alternate-uses task only, avoid list written by the experimenters from common uses. The planned comparison in Exp 2 is marginal.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: a supplied list of the common answers plus an avoid line works for people when the list is verbal and specific. The unit is a concrete list of old answers, not a general 'be original'.

source: Feng, Helie, Panchal (2025) Enhancing design concept diversity: multi-persona prompting strategies for large language models (Design Science)
finding: Gap 1. At the same number of concepts (25 concepts, 125 professional terms), how the prompt is organised matters. One prompt listing all five personas gave the least diverse set. Five parallel prompts (one persona each) beat no persona. A sequence of update prompts matched parallel prompting when the persona order was good.
numbers: GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-flash, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct. Hypothesis 3a: 25 concepts with no persona vs 5 x 5 with five personas: parallel higher diversity for each model. Hypotheses 3b and 3c: collective prompt lowest; parallel about equal to sequential with the best of five orders. Updating an existing set with a new persona raised diversity only for Gemini-1.5-flash, not GPT-4o or Llama. Mean diversity scores for one problem across five persona orders: 0.525 to 0.547 (SD about 0.02). Other mean differences are in figures, not extracted.
limits: Diversity is measured by an LLM summarising concepts into professional terms plus a semantic score; no human judgment, no quality score. Later sequential steps matched only the current persona's knowledge base, not earlier personas, so 'update' replaced rather than integrated. Tokens not equal across strategies.
agent_relevance: Splitting one request into several independent, differently framed calls beats one crowded prompt. Updating a draft with a new frame did little for two of three models.

source: Ege, Ovrebo, Stubberud, Berg, Elverum, Steinert, Vestad (2025) ChatGPT as an inventor (AI EDAM 39:e6)
finding: Gap 3. In a 48-hour prototyping hackathon, ChatGPT 4.0 directed one team of two people against five human teams. The authors report design fixation in the model: it kept refining one concept after returns shrank, and it fixed on details in its prompt (for example the last machine in a list of manufacturing options). When the team told it 'we have reached a plateau in performance', it was willing to pivot.
numbers: Six teams; the ChatGPT team finished second, firing its NERF dart 14.8 m against a team average of 12.0 m. Qualitative coding (21 of 53 codes for that team were problem solving). The authors' key finding KF 9 states the fixation.
quote: ChatGPT experiences and is limited by design fixation
limits: One run, one task, qualitative judgement by the authors, no counts of repeated concepts. Humans acted as hands. Not a controlled test of context effects.
agent_relevance: A plain external signal ('performance plateaued, test one of the original ideas') broke the fixation. A code-side plateau detector that forces a return to an earlier branch is cheap.

source: Sio, Kotovsky, Cagan (2015) Fixation or inspiration? A meta-analytic review of the role of examples on design processes (Design Studies 39)
finding: Gap 6. NOT opened. Publisher pages (ScienceDirect, Elsevier linking hub, ResearchGate) blocked automated access, OpenAlex lists no open copy, and Semantic Scholar returns the abstract as elided. The only text I saw is a machine-generated Semantic Scholar one-line summary, which I treat as unverified.
numbers: Machine summary (unverified): examples led to more example-related ideas and fewer idea categories, but the ideas were more novel, and solution quality correlated positively with copying from examples. About 191 citations in OpenAlex. No moderator effect sizes obtained.
limits: Not read. The study count (43 in earlier notes) and effect sizes by moderator remain unchecked.
agent_relevance: Do not treat 'examples raise novelty and quality' as verified.

source: Deng, Brucks, Toubia (2026) Examining and Addressing Barriers to Diversity in LLM-Generated Ideas, measurement and temperature (re-opened)
finding: Gaps 1 and 10. Their fixation slope rests on one LLM coder. GPT-4o labels each idea on three dimensions, merges labels into a hierarchy, and relabels. No human second coder or agreement figure is reported, and the authors list human raters for quality as future work. Raising temperature did not close the gap to humans.
numbers: Temperature test on the same 990 ideas: default 1.0 gives 22 categories and 88 unique combinations; 1.5 gives 23 and 99; humans give 28 and 206. At temperature 2.0 outputs were often garbled and could not be categorised. The idea generator and the coder are both GPT-4o.
quote: Rigorous evaluations using human raters would complement the findings of this paper
limits: Same model family generates and codes, so a shared bias could shrink or inflate category counts. No inter-coder reliability. One domain (fitness products).
agent_relevance: The category-accumulation slope has unmeasured judge noise. If the agent uses it as a probe, fix the category list in advance and check coder stability by recoding with a second model.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou, Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation (arXiv 2505.06120)
finding: Gap 3. In multi-turn tasks, models propose a first answer too early and then rely on it. Later answers grow longer instead of replacing the old assumptions. Repeating the instructions (recap or snowball) helped only partly.
numbers: 200,000+ simulated conversations, six tasks. Average drop of 39% from single-turn to multi-turn; the loss splits into a small aptitude loss (about 15%) and a large rise in unreliability (+112%). Answer bloat: final multi-turn answers 20 to 300% longer; correct code from sharded conversations 850 vs 668 characters (27% longer), correct SQL 129 vs 113 (14% longer). Snowball (repeat all prior user information each turn) recovered 15 to 20% of the single-turn to multi-turn drop; Recap on the last turn did a little better but is not realistic.
quote: overly rely on previous (incorrect) answer attempts
limits: Instruction-following tasks with underspecified prompts, not idea generation. 'Relies on previous attempts' is the authors' reading of bloat. Recap test used GPT-4o and GPT-4o-mini only.
agent_relevance: Supports restarting from a clean statement of the task rather than appending to an old thread, with only a short note on what failed.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gap 1. Critique-and-edit by the same model with no outside signal made reasoning answers worse, and the earlier gains in the literature came from oracle labels that told the model when to stop. Multi-agent debate was no better than self-consistency at an equal number of responses.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA: 75.8 at one call, 38.1 after one self-correction round (3 calls), 41.8 after two (5 calls). GSM8K 75.9, 75.1, 74.7. GPT-4 CommonSenseQA 82.0, 79.5, 80.0; GSM8K 95.5, 91.5, 89.0. GPT-4-Turbo GSM8K 91.5, 88.0, 90.0. Llama-2 GSM8K 62.0, 43.5, 36.5. With oracle labels self-correction improved results.
quote: without the use of oracle labels, self-correction consistently results in a decrease in performance
limits: Reasoning and QA with a single right answer, 2023 models. Creative editing was not tested. The failure comes from a correct answer being changed to a wrong one, which works differently when there is no key.
agent_relevance: A critique-and-edit step needs an external check (code, test, held-out variant) to pay for itself. Without one, count it as costing tokens and possibly quality.

source: Peeperkorn, Kouwenhoven, Brown, Jordanous (2024) Is Temperature the Creativity Parameter of Large Language Models? (ICCC 2024)
finding: Gap 1. Temperature is a weak lever for novelty in story generation, and it lowers coherence.
numbers: Llama 2-Chat 70B, 100 stories at each of 7 temperatures, plus an exemplar greedy story; 36 human raters, each assigned 5 of 31 stories. Temperature weakly correlated with novelty, moderately and negatively with coherence, no relationship with cohesion or typicality.
quote: temperature is weakly correlated with novelty
limits: One model, one narrative prompt, 36 raters; correlation values are in the text but I did not extract them.
agent_relevance: Raising temperature is not a substitute for a structural defixation step. Consistent with the Deng temperature test.

source: Tian et al. (2024) MacGyver (re-opened to check baselines)
finding: Gap 7. The MacGyver prompting comparison uses three arms: a vanilla prompt, iterative step-wise self-reflection, and divergent-convergent thinking. There is no plain chain-of-thought arm and no matched-token arm.
numbers: 180 problems, GPT-4, Claude2, Llama2-13b. Self-reflect cut infeasible solutions by 9.7% vs 4.3% for divergent-convergent; divergent-convergent raised efficient solutions by 6.5% vs 2.2% (as in c05). Vanilla is the reference.
limits: Cannot say whether affordance reflection beats plain chain of thought. Gjerde et al. (2025) found GPT-4o with CoT matched humans on a four-option tool-choice version, so a CoT baseline is likely to close part of the gap.
agent_relevance: Before adopting an affordance-check step, test it against zero-shot CoT with equal tokens on MacGyver or a tool-substitution multiple-choice set.
